safetyNote: Fusarium oxysporum in the broad sense of the FOSC includes plant-pathogenic lineages as well as non-pathogenic lineages. This microscopic mould is not a mushroom for food identification. Morphology alone may not reliably identify it to species or pathogenic form.

sections.title: Name and diversity
sections.text: Fusarium oxysporum is a name historically applied to a highly diverse group generally called the Fusarium oxysporum species complex (FOSC). It includes plant-pathogenic lineages as well as non-pathogenic ones. Forma specialis names designate groups associated with particular hosts or symptoms; they do not necessarily represent separate species. The taxonomic boundaries of the complex are being revised using phylogenetic data.

sections.title: Colony and hyphae
sections.text: In culture, colonies may be cottony or floccose, often initially white, with cream, pink, violet or sometimes deeper pigmentation depending on strain, medium and incubation. Hyphae are hyaline, branched and septate. Colony colour is variable and cannot identify the species by itself.

sections.title: Three asexual spore types
sections.text: Microconidia are small, ellipsoidal to slightly fusiform, usually nonseptate or with one septum, and often gathered in small false heads on phialides. Macroconidia are larger, hyaline, falcate to slightly curved, most often three- or four-septate in the reference description, with a pedicellate or foot-shaped basal cell. Chlamydospores are globose, thick-walled, terminal or intercalary, solitary, paired or sometimes in short chains; they contribute to survival in soil. Their presence and abundance vary among strains and culture conditions.

sections.title: Ecology and diagnostic limits
sections.text: The complex is widely associated with soils and roots. Some lineages colonize vascular tissues and cause wilt in host plants, while others live without causing disease. Microscopic characters and the affected host alone cannot resolve every lineage in the complex; precise identification may require molecular methods and reference cultures. It does not produce a macroscopic cap-and-stem fruit body.

sections.title: Reading the plate
sections.text: The white-background scientific plate combines a Petri-dish colony with documented, schematic microscopic views: ellipsoidal microconidia in small false heads, septate falcate macroconidia, and globose thick-walled chlamydospores on or between septate hyphae. The views use different scales; the colony is not shown at the same scale as the microscopic structures.

traits: Microscopic soil mould, with no cap-and-stem fruit body.
Ellipsoidal microconidia, usually 0–1 septum, often in false heads.
Falcate or slightly curved, usually multiseptate macroconidia.
Globose, thick-walled terminal or intercalary chlamydospores used for persistence.
Colony pigmentation varies with strain and culture conditions.
